sentences.text: The adult holotype specimen IGM 100/11 measured approximately 6 meters in length and stood 1.9 meters tall at the hip.
This dinosaur had a long skull with a gently convex upper profile compared to other members of its family.
Gallimimus possessed 64 to 66 vertebrae in its spine, a count lower than that of other ornithomimids.
The animal held its neck at an oblique angle of 35 degrees.
Gallimimus is the largest known member of the ornithomimid group of dinosaurs.
A fossil trackway associated with a clenched Gallimimus foot was reported in 2017 based on a discovery made in 2009.
Gallimimus was featured in the 1993 movie Jurassic Park directed by Steven Spielberg.
The Gallimimus in Jurassic Park were animated using footage of ostriches and herding gazelles as references.
Fossils of Gallimimus were discovered in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia during the 1960s by Polish-Mongolian expeditions.
Polish-Mongolian paleontological expeditions to the Gobi Desert were organized between 1963 and 1965.
The genus Gallimimus was named by Osmólska and colleagues in 1972.
In 1988, Gregory S. Paul reclassified the species as Ornithomimus bullatus based on skull similarities among ornithomimids.
Gallimimus was a fast-running animal estimated to reach speeds of 42 to 56 km/h (29 to 34 mph) to escape predators.
Paleontologist Dale Russell suggested in 1972 that Gallimimus was a fast, cursorial animal that used speed to escape predators.
Gallimimus was adapted for running due to its light build and long hind legs.
Evidence from a bone bed suggests Gallimimus may have lived in groups.
Researchers suggest Gallimimus had a highly mobile front neck and rigid hind neck, similar to chickens, which likely aided in locating ground prey.
The beak of Gallimimus resembled that of a duck or goose, and it likely swallowed small living prey whole.
Researchers suggested Gallimimus had weak arms compared to other ornithomimosaurs like Deinocheirus.
Gallimimus skulls changed during growth, with the rear and orbits shrinking while the snout lengthened, similar to modern crocodiles.
In 2012, Zelenitsky and colleagues concluded adult ornithomimosaur arm structures were likely secondary sexual characteristics used for courtship, display, or brooding.
Gallimimus belongs to the family Ornithomimidae, which is part of the group Ornithomimosauria.
In 1976, Barsbold established the new group Ornithomimosauria to contain the family Ornithomimidae.
Gallimimus is classified within the infraorder Ornithomimosauria.
Gallimimus lived about 70 million years ago during the early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
After the separation of Europe from Asia by the Turgai Strait, ornithomimosaurs like Gallimimus were largely restricted to Asia and North America.
There is an ongoing debate regarding the diet of Gallimimus, with theories ranging from carnivory to herbivory and filter-feeding.
It is debated whether structures in Gallimimus's beak were used for water filter-feeding or for processing tough plant material.
In 2005, Paul Barrett argued that Gallimimus beak structures were likely rigid ridges like those in turtles and hadrosaurs rather than flexible filter-feeding bristles.
The function of pneumatization in Gallimimus is debated, with hypotheses including mass reduction, high metabolism, balance, or thermoregulation.
